title: What is Jan Aushadhi?
questions: are jan aushadhi medicines good quality
answer: Jan Aushadhi (Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana, PMBJP) is a Government of India scheme run by the Pharmaceuticals & Medical Devices Bureau of India (PMBI) under the Department of Pharmaceuticals. Its Kendras (stores) sell generic medicines that are usually far cheaper than branded equivalents. The scheme states that its medicines are tested for quality at NABL-accredited laboratories before supply. MediBot shows a Jan Aushadhi option when its composition is identical to the medicine you asked about, and can find Kendras near your pincode.

title: Are generic medicines as effective as branded ones?
questions: are generic medicines as effective as branded
sasti dawai kaam karti hai kya
answer: In India every medicine, branded or generic, must meet the same quality standards under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. A generic with the same active ingredients, strength, dosage form and release type is expected to work the same way; it is usually cheaper because it carries no brand-marketing cost. Inactive ingredients (fillers, colours) can differ. For a few medicines where small differences matter (for example thyroid medicines, blood thinners and anti-epileptics), doctors may prefer that you stay on one brand. Always confirm any switch with your doctor or pharmacist.

title: What is a Schedule H (prescription) medicine?
questions: why do i need a prescription
what does rx mean on medicine
answer: Under the Drugs Rules, 1945, Schedule H medicines may be sold by a chemist only against the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner; their packs carry the Rx symbol and a warning to that effect. Schedule H1 (for example many newer antibiotics, some sleeping pills and anti-TB medicines) adds stricter controls: the pharmacist must record the prescriber, the patient and the medicine in a register. Schedule X covers narcotic and psychotropic medicines with the strictest controls. These rules exist because such medicines can be harmful without a doctor's supervision.

title: What does the red line on a medicine pack mean?
questions: what is red line on antibiotic
answer: In 2016 the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare started the 'Medicines with the Red Line' campaign: a vertical red line on a pack (used for antibiotics and other prescription-only medicines) means it should be taken only when a doctor prescribes it. Do not buy or use such medicines on your own, and do not share leftovers.
source: MoHFW 'Medicines with the Red Line' campaign; WHO fact sheet on antimicrobial resistance

title: Using antibiotics responsibly
questions: can i take antibiotics without prescription
answer: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections; they do not work against viruses such as those causing colds and flu. Using them when not needed, or not as prescribed, helps bacteria become resistant (antimicrobial resistance), which WHO lists among the top global public-health threats. WHO advises using antibiotics only when prescribed by a certified health professional, following the health worker's advice on how to take them, never sharing them and not using leftovers.

title: What are banned FDCs?
answer: A fixed-dose combination (FDC) contains two or more active ingredients in one product. Under Section 26A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 the Government can prohibit medicines it finds lacking therapeutic justification or risky. Hundreds of FDCs have been prohibited by notification (for example 328 in 2018, 14 in 2023 and 156 in 2024), some subject to court cases. MediBot checks every product against these notifications and never suggests a banned product.

title: Can a pharmacy charge more than the MRP or the ceiling price?
answer: No retailer may charge more than the MRP printed on the pack. For essential medicines (the National List of Essential Medicines), the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) fixes ceiling prices under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, and the MRP of such products must not exceed the ceiling (plus applicable GST). Overcharging can be reported to NPPA through its Pharma Jan Samadhan grievance system. MediBot flags live prices above the NPPA ceiling.

title: How do I report a side effect?
answer: In India, side effects (adverse drug reactions) can be reported to the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI), run by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, through its toll-free helpline 1800-180-3024 or the ADR PvPI mobile app. Tell your doctor too. If a reaction is severe (swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, fainting), call 112 or go to the nearest hospital immediately.

title: How can I consult a doctor for free?
answer: eSanjeevani is the Government of India's free national telemedicine service: you can consult a doctor online by video from your phone or computer, and receive an e-prescription where appropriate. Government health centres (PHCs, CHCs and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs) also offer consultations. MediBot cannot prescribe; a registered doctor must decide which medicine you need.

title: Mental health support
questions: i feel depressed who can i talk to
answer: Tele-MANAS is the Government of India's free, confidential 24x7 mental-health helpline: call 14416 or 1-800-891-4416 to talk to a trained counsellor in your language. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 112.

title: Emergency numbers in India
answer: Call 112 (national emergency number) or 108 (ambulance in most states). For a suspected poisoning or overdose, call for help immediately and keep the medicine pack with you so the doctors know what was taken. Do not wait for symptoms to appear.

title: What does ORS do in diarrhoea?
answer: Oral rehydration solution (ORS) is a mixture of clean water, salts and sugar. In diarrhoea the body loses water and salts; ORS is absorbed in the small intestine and replaces them, which WHO describes as the cornerstone of treating dehydration from diarrhoea. WHO also advises continuing to eat (and breastfeeding infants) and, for children, zinc supplements as advised by a health worker. Get medical help urgently if there is blood in the stool, the person cannot drink, is very sleepy, has sunken eyes or is passing very little urine.

title: How should I store medicines?
questions: where to keep medicines at home
answer: Keep medicines in their original pack, in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight, heat and damp (bathrooms and windowsills are poor places), and out of the sight and reach of children. Some medicines must be kept in a refrigerator; this is printed on the pack or leaflet. Do not use a medicine whose colour, smell or texture has changed; ask your pharmacist.
source: NHS – Storing medicines at home (United Lincolnshire Hospitals)

title: How long can I use a syrup or eye drops after opening?
questions: how long can i use eye drops after opening
syrup kitne din chalega khulne ke baad
answer: The expiry date on the pack applies to the unopened product. Many liquids, creams and especially eye drops have a shorter 'use within ... of opening' period printed on the label or leaflet (eye drops commonly within about four weeks of opening). Follow that instruction, write the opening date on the bottle, and ask your pharmacist if the label does not say. Do not use a medicine that has changed colour, smell or consistency.
source: NHS – Storing medicines at home (United Lincolnshire Hospitals)

title: Can I use expired medicines?
questions: how to dispose of old medicines
what to do with unused medicines
answer: Do not use medicines past their expiry date: they may be less effective or, rarely, harmful. To dispose of them, use a take-back option if one is available (some pharmacies and hospitals collect them); otherwise follow the disposal instructions on the leaflet. If there are none, the US FDA suggests mixing the medicine (without crushing tablets) with something unappealing such as used tea leaves or soil, sealing it in a bag and putting it in household waste, and removing personal details from the label.
source: US FDA – Where and how to dispose of unused medicines

title: What should I do if I miss a dose?
questions: what if i miss a dose
answer: First check the patient leaflet in the pack: it usually says what to do for that medicine. As general guidance, the NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service says never to take two doses together to make up for a missed one. For some medicines (for example insulin, anti-epileptics, blood thinners, contraceptives) a missed dose needs specific advice, so contact your doctor or pharmacist.
source: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service – Missed doses

title: What is an over-the-counter (OTC) medicine in India?
questions: which medicines can i buy without prescription
answer: Indian law does not yet have a separate legal 'OTC' list: medicines are either in a prescription schedule (H, H1, X and others) or not, and Schedule K lists certain household remedies that may be sold more freely. A draft list of OTC medicines was published in 2022. Even for non-prescription medicines, read the label, and ask a pharmacist or doctor if you have other conditions, are pregnant, or are giving it to a child. MediBot treats any medicine it cannot verify as non-prescription as prescription-only.
source: CDSCO – Drugs Rules, 1945 (Schedule K); G.S.R. 393(E), 2022 draft

title: Who regulates vitamins and supplements?
answer: Most vitamins, minerals and health supplements sold as foods (nutraceuticals) are regulated by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), not as drugs; high-strength vitamin products sold as medicines are regulated by CDSCO. Supplements can still interact with medicines or be harmful in excess, so tell your doctor about any supplement you take.

title: Does MediBot cover Ayurvedic or homeopathic medicines?
answer: MediBot covers modern (allopathic) medicines and supplements in Indian pharmacy catalogues. Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH) medicines are regulated under the Ministry of AYUSH and are not compared here. Herbal products can also interact with modern medicines, so tell your doctor about them.

title: Can I split, crush or chew a tablet?
questions: can i break tablet in half
tablet tod ke kha sakte hai
answer: Only if the label or your pharmacist says so. Tablets with special coatings or release systems (marked SR, ER, CR, XR, MR, DR or EC, and many stomach-protecting tablets) are usually meant to be swallowed whole: crushing or splitting them can release too much medicine at once or destroy it in the stomach. A score line does not always mean a tablet may be split. Ask your pharmacist, who can suggest a liquid or other form if swallowing is difficult.

title: How does MediBot choose cheaper alternatives?
answer: MediBot suggests an alternative only when its active composition is identical: the same ingredients, the same strength of each, the same dosage form and the same release type (for example SR vs normal). Banned products are never suggested. Prices are compared per tablet, ml or gram, from live pharmacy product pages where available (otherwise a dated price, labelled as such). Please confirm any switch with your doctor or pharmacist.

title: How do I buy medicines online safely?
questions: is it safe to buy medicine online
answer: Buy only from licensed pharmacies. A legitimate pharmacy, online or offline, asks for a valid prescription before selling prescription (Rx, Schedule H/H1) medicines and shows its drug licence details and a registered pharmacist. Be wary of sites that sell prescription medicines without a prescription or at prices that look too good to be true. Check the pack, batch number, expiry date and MRP on delivery.
source: CDSCO – Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 (licensed sale)

title: How do I read a medicine pack?
questions: what is batch number on medicine
what is written on medicine strip
answer: An Indian medicine pack shows the brand and generic (active ingredient) names with the strength of each ingredient, the manufacturer and licence number, batch number, manufacturing and expiry dates, and the MRP (inclusive of taxes). Prescription medicines carry Rx and a Schedule H/H1 warning; some antibiotics carry a red line. Comparing the generic names and strengths is how you can tell whether two brands are the same medicine.

title: Can I take antacids with milk, food or other medicines?
questions: can i take antacids with milk
answer: The NHS advises that antacids work best taken with or soon after food, when indigestion and heartburn are most likely, and that their effect may last longer when taken with food. Antacids can affect how well other medicines work, so the NHS advises not to take other medicines within 2 to 4 hours of an antacid. Antacids are not meant for regular long-term use: speak to a doctor if you need them often, and ask a pharmacist first if you are pregnant, have kidney, liver or heart problems, are on a low-salt diet, or are choosing one for a child under 12. For a specific antacid, check its leaflet or ask your pharmacist.
